html:
The Cherokee, or Tsalagi, are an Indigenous people of the Southeastern Woodlands. Before the 1700s they lived in towns along the river valleys of the southern Appalachians, in what is now western North Carolina, eastern Tennessee, northern Georgia and nearby states.

Their language is Iroquoian, related to that of the Haudenosaunee far to the north. They farmed maize, beans and squash and hunted deer. Hernando de Soto passed through their lands in 1540; in the 1700s they traded deerskins with the British in Carolina.

In the early 1800s many Cherokee took up European American ways to keep their land. Sequoyah created the Cherokee syllabary in 1821, the nation printed its own newspaper and wrote a constitution in 1827. It did not save them. Under the Indian Removal Act, the army forced most Cherokee west to Indian Territory in 1838 and 1839, on the Trail of Tears. Thousands died.

Today there are three federally recognized tribes: the Cherokee Nation and the United Keetoowah Band in Oklahoma, and the Eastern Band in North Carolina.
